summary:
Kahramanmaraş stands under Turkish national law, and the source inventory records no Kahramanmaraş-specific statute, incident or court case concerning trans people. What a trans visitor faces in the province is the national framework as it operates elsewhere in Türkiye.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal code to imprison for up to three years anyone who incites or promotes conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with penalties of up to four years, and restrict gender-affirming healthcare to people aged 25 and over under mandatory permanent infertility, exposing providers to fines and up to seven years and patients to up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected to the draft. The package is national legislation and applies to the province; it had not been enacted when reported.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', records 313 liberty violations, roughly 2.5 times the previous year and mostly detentions, together with 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 and mostly linked to peaceful assembly, and six right-to-life violations of which three were recorded as hate-motivated killings with trans people most affected. Because the state keeps no hate-crime statistics, these figures are counted from media and civil-society reports.

Identity checks are the ordinary point of contact between a trans visitor and the authorities. On 31 July 2025 police in the Beyoğlu district of Istanbul carried out mass ID roundups of trans women, recording their names and filming video. Foreign nationals are required to produce original photo identification at transit checkpoints, so any stop becomes an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation.
tangentialFactors:
The Istanbul roundups of 31 July 2025 are a single data point illustrating a national pattern rather than a local characteristic of Kahramanmaraş; the source records no Kahramanmaraş-specific finding for that incident or for the Kaos GL counts.

Kaos GL attributes the 2025 escalation to hostility institutionalised as state policy under 'Year of the Family' instructions issued to public institutions, hate speech from senior officials, and the cancellation or banning of artistic events. The findings describe national practice rather than provincial choice.

The draft 11th Judicial Package was still pending when Human Rights Watch reported it, so its provisions are not yet law; the objection of fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association indicates organised domestic resistance to the measures but does not suspend them.

The marriage-ceremony offence in the draft would reach a trans visitor travelling with a partner, since participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony is the conduct penalised rather than the traveller's own gender status.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kahramanmaraş are subject to the same national penal-code amendments proposed in the 11th Judicial Package as visitors, with the healthcare restrictions falling on patients as well as providers: people under 25, or those unwilling to accept permanent infertility, would lose lawful access to gender-affirming care under the draft.

Kaos GL's 2025 counts — six right-to-life violations with three recorded as hate-motivated killings, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, 313 liberty violations — are compiled from media and civil-society reporting because the Turkish state maintains no hate-crime statistics, so official data will not corroborate or contradict them.

The Turkish Medical Association joined fifteen LGBT groups in objecting to the draft package, and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular and the Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 that barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option in e-reports affect the records of resident trans patients as much as anyone else.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kahramanmaraş-specific statute, incident, arrest or court case appears anywhere in the source inventory; every finding here is national in scope or drawn from another province, and local enforcement practice in Kahramanmaraş is not sourced.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted since the Human Rights Watch report of 29 October 2025 is unresolved in the inventory, which records the draft as pending at the time of reporting.

The inventory does not establish how identity checkpoints operate in Kahramanmaraş itself, nor whether passport-gender-marker mismatches have produced documented refusals of entry or detention in the province; the 31 July 2025 roundups are sourced only to Beyoğlu, Istanbul.
